A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-concept interpretability study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching content across the substantial reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original concept-identification, sparse-probing, and steering experiments on Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B, including supplementary experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports steering evaluations using both correlation-based and gradient-attribution-based feature selection.

M1.justification: The steering procedure adds selection by activation–concept correlation as its main feature-selection rule; v1 primarily selects by gradient attribution. Gradient selection remains in v2 Appendix I.2. The SAE architectures, training objectives, and reconstruction-corrected steering operation remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage narrows for steering under alternative concept correlations: v1 Appendix J evaluates steering after correlating past tense with passive voice, whereas v2 retains only the MCC evaluation for this condition. The underlying PCFG corpus, four concepts, and main science-domain/positive-sentiment setting remain.

E2.justification: Removing v1 Figure 16 eliminates the supplementary steering comparison involving SpADE. V2's steering comparisons contain ReLU, Top-K, and SSAE. Comparator membership in the retained MCC, DCI-ES, and sparse-probing experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: The central steering evaluation changes from gradient-selected features to correlation-selected features, with attribution selection retained as an alternative evaluation. This changes which features the causal tests interrogate and underlies replacement main results. The reported training-set size also changes from 382,884 to 382,459 sentences; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects regeneration or correction. The 1,007-example test set and principal training budgets remain.

E4.justification: The steering robustness evidence is substantially reworked: v2 compares correlation-based and attribution-based selection, while retaining earlier attribution analyses in Appendix I.2. It removes v1's detailed individual-versus-joint steering coefficient curves and the alternate tense/voice-correlation steering test. Feature-splitting and probe-validation analyses remain, and the qualitative generations are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: V2 fills a missing uncertainty entry in Table 4: Pythia SSAE variance explained at correlation 0.0 changes from 99.6 to 99.6 (0.0). Otherwise, the three-seed reporting and one-standard-deviation bands remain; no increased run count or new statistical procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Main steering plots and Tables 1–2 report replacement results under correlation selection. For example, Table 1's Pythia Top-K mean independence/selectivity at correlation 0.1 changes from 0.29/0.27 to 0.60/0.84 under the different selector. The corresponding gradient disjointness plot also changes: v2 Figure 16 no longer shows the large off-diagonal Pythia sentiment ReLU point in v1 Figure 5. Main MCC/DCI plots, probe-accuracy heatmaps, and qualitative generations are retained.

T1.justification: V2 removes invertibility from the linear-recoverability assumption and rewrites the formal disjointness equality using log-probability differences instead of probability differences. Its new Section 2 disentanglement formula omits the row normalization specified in retained Appendix D.2, introducing an inconsistency. Appendix C's identifiability definitions and the SAE objective equations remain unchanged; no new proofs appear.

C1.justification: V1's categorical abstract statement that features correspond to no more than one concept becomes the qualified claim that features are typically sensitive to only one concept. The central contributions remain: controlled multi-concept evaluation, feature splitting, and evidence that correlational disentanglement and nearly additive steering effects do not establish selective control.

C2.justification: V1 recommends investigating spurious correlates; v2 suggests an appropriate architecture can tolerate most correlations except near-complete ones. V2 also explains why attribution-selected features have larger effects but lower selectivity, and develops implications for circuit overlap, orthogonality, and counterfactual-independence objectives. V1's intrinsic-dimensionality discussion is removed, while the main dataset and applicability limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code/data access link and documents concept sampling, upsampling, and conditional terminal sampling more explicitly. It also identifies Pearson correlation and impurity-based feature importances. These are additional disclosures; they do not establish changes to the underlying implementations. Most training hyperparameters and probe details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 removes the compositional-generalization subsection and its associated citations, and adds discussion of Joshi et al. (2026) on evaluating identifiability. It gives causal abstraction a more explicit role in future research. The principal positioning against single-concept interpretability evaluations and within causal representation learning remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental explanations, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. V2 adds a Preliminaries section, reorganizes metric explanations, separates the steering-selection variants into appendix subsections, and adds an AI-tools disclosure. These changes substantially revise the narrative structure beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the document into two columns, replaces Figure 1's causal graph with a study overview, reformats steering graphics, and extensively rearranges figures and tables. The unchanged generation examples become Figure 18, Figure 7's diagrams are stacked, and misleading headers in Tables 2 and 5 are corrected.

improvement.justification: V2 modestly strengthens the central argument by steering the same correlation-selected features used for identification and retaining attribution-based checks. Clearer organization and added code/data access information improve usability. These gains are limited by removal of supplementary steering checks and the new inconsistency between Section 2's disentanglement formula and Appendix D.2; the revision does not resolve the study's broader applicability limitations.
